{{Short description|Theorem in topology}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Kuratowski's intersection theorem''' is a result in [[general topology]] that gives a sufficient condition for a nested sequence of sets to have a non-empty [[intersection]].  Kuratowski's result is a generalisation of [[Cantor's intersection theorem]].  Whereas Cantor's result requires that the sets involved be [[compact space|compact]], Kuratowski's result allows them to be non-compact, but insists that their non-compactness "tends to zero" in an appropriate sense.  The theorem is named for the [[Polish people|Polish]] [[mathematician]] [[Kazimierz Kuratowski]], who proved it in 1930.

== Statement of the theorem ==

Let (''X'', ''d'') be a [[complete metric space]].  Given a subset ''A''&nbsp;&sube;&nbsp;''X'', its [[measure of non-compactness|'''Kuratowski measure of non-compactness''']] ''α''(''A'')&nbsp;&ge;&nbsp;0 is defined by
:<math>\alpha(A) = \inf \left\{ r \geq 0 \left| \begin{array}{c} A \text{ can be covered by finitely many subsets} \\ \text{of } X \text{, each with diameter at most } r \end{array} \right. \right\}.</math>
Note that, if ''A'' is itself compact, then ''α''(''A'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, since every cover of ''A'' by open balls of arbitrarily small diameter will have a finite subcover.  The converse is also true: if ''α''(''A'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, then ''A'' must be [[relatively compact set|precompact]], and indeed compact if ''A'' is closed.  Also, if ''A'' is a subset of ''B'', then ''α''(''A'')&nbsp;&le;&nbsp;''α''(''B'').  In some sense, the quantity ''α''(''A'') is a numerical description of "how non-compact" the set ''A'' is.

Now consider a sequence of sets ''A''<sub>''n''</sub>&nbsp;&sube;&nbsp;''X'', one for each natural number ''n''.  '''Kuratowski's intersection theorem''' asserts that if these sets are non-empty, [[closed set|closed]], decreasingly nested (i.e. ''A''<sub>''n''+1</sub>&nbsp;&sube;&nbsp;''A''<sub>''n''</sub> for each ''n''), and ''α''(''A''<sub>''n''</sub>)&nbsp;→&nbsp;0 as ''n''&nbsp;→&nbsp;&infin;, then their infinite intersection
:<math>\bigcap_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_{n}</math>
is a non-empty compact set.

The result also holds if one works with the ball measure of non-compactness or the separation measure of non-compactness, since these three measures of non-compactness are mutually Lipschitz equivalent;  if any one of them tends to zero as ''n''&nbsp;→&nbsp;&infin;, then so must the other two.
